questions.lead_in: Based on the Gram stain, what is the most appropriate stain to perform?
questions.explanation: Modified acid-fast The Gram stain shows filamentous beaded gram-positive rods, indicative of an aerobic actinomycete, most closely resembling Nocardia. A modified acid-fast stain would be positive for Nocardia. A positive modified acid-fast stain result would not provide a definitive diagnosis since other aerobic actinomycetes can be modified acid-fast positive. However, based on the other factors, it supports the diagnosis of nocardiosis while waiting for the organism to grow in culture. The acid-fast stain is for Mycobacterium spp. Nocardia will stain negative with the acid-fast stain, as it uses a stronger decolorizing agent. Giemsa, periodic acid–Schiff, and Warthin–Starry are histopathology stains that are unrelated to the diagnosis of aerobic actinomycetes.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q1

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman was admitted with pneumonia following influenza A infection. IV ceftriaxone was started empirically. Investigations: Sputum culture: Staphylococcus aureus isolated; resistant to clindamycin, sensitive to oxacillin, trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX), and vancomycin
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate method for ceftriaxone susceptibility testing?
questions.explanation: Susceptibility can be inferred Oxacillin is an indicator drug for determining MSSA vs. MRSA. Breakpoints do not exist for other beta-lactam drugs for staphylococci, and testing other beta-lactams can lead to inaccurate results. Oxacillin-susceptible staphylococci are susceptible to nafcillin, cephalosporins, beta-lactam/ beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations, and carbapenems. Because the isolate is susceptible to oxacillin, it can be inferred that it is also susceptible to ceftriaxone.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q1

questions.question: Gram stains.

parts.text: Describe the method.
4 organisms that don't stain well.
2 organisms that tend to overdecolourize
What are 2 tests that can be done to differentiate a gram positive from a gram negative organism (if the stain is equivocal)?

questions.model_answer:
a) Method: heat- or methanol-fix smear; (1) crystal violet primary stain; (2) Gram's iodine mordant (forms crystal violet-iodine complex); (3) decolourize with acetone-alcohol; (4) counterstain with safranin. Gram-positive organisms retain the CV-iodine complex (thick peptidoglycan, low lipid) and stain purple/blue; gram-negative organisms decolourize and take up safranin, staining pink/red.
b) 4 organisms that stain poorly with Gram stain: (1) Mycobacterium spp. (high mycolic acid content - need acid-fast stain), (2) Legionella spp., (3) Treponema and other spirochetes (too thin to visualize), (4) Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma (no cell wall).
c) 2 organisms prone to overdecolourization (appear gram-variable/negative despite being gram-positive): (1) Bacteroides fragilis and other anaerobic gram-negative-appearing organisms are not the issue - rather: Clostridium spp. (esp. older cultures), (2) Bacillus spp. (also can overdecolourize in older colonies); Gardnerella vaginalis is also classically gram-variable.
d) 2 tests to differentiate gram-positive vs gram-negative when stain is equivocal: (1) KOH string test (gram-negative cell wall lyses in 3% KOH producing a mucoid string when loop is lifted; gram-positive does not), (2) vancomycin susceptibility disk / L-alanine aminopeptidase (LAP) test (gram-positive susceptible to vancomycin and LAP-negative; gram-negative resistant to vancomycin and LAP-positive).
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard clinical microbiology procedure (CLSI/ASM Manual of Clinical Microbiology), not covered as a discrete Mandell chapter.

questions.question: A lung biopsy is sent from a patient who is immunocompromised. They are concerned about a fungal infection and have sent for fungal culture.

parts.text: How would you process the specimen in the lab?
What are 3 media you would use and provide a rationale for each?
What are 2 media you could use to enhance sporulation?

questions.model_answer:
a) Processing: grind/homogenize tissue, inoculate a portion directly onto multiple fungal media, prepare a direct KOH/calcofluor white smear and Gram stain for morphology, and consider histopathology (GMS/PAS) submission in parallel.
b) 3 media with rationale: (1) Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) - general-purpose recovery of most fungi; (2) Inhibitory mould agar or SDA with chloramphenicol/gentamicin - suppresses bacterial overgrowth from contaminated/non-sterile-adjacent sites; (3) Brain-heart infusion agar with blood, with and without cycloheximide - supports recovery of dimorphic/fastidious fungi (cycloheximide-free plate needed since some pathogens e.g. Aspergillus, Cryptococcus are cycloheximide-sensitive).
c) 2 media to enhance sporulation: (1) Potato dextrose agar (PDA), (2) Cornmeal agar (with Tween 80).
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard mycology laboratory processing (Clinical Microbiology Procedures Handbook), not a Mandell topic.

questions.question: Expected susceptibilities for the following organisms (just say S or R)

parts.text: Staph aureus and penicillin
Morganella and imipenem
Stenotrophomonas and septra
Burkholderia and colistin
Klebsiella and ampicillin

questions.model_answer: (1) Staph aureus + penicillin: R (intrinsic via penicillinase, >90% of isolates). (2) Morganella + imipenem: S (carbapenems active against Morganella, though intrinsic imipenem MICs can be modestly elevated - generally reported S). (3) Stenotrophomonas + septra (TMP-SMX): S (drug of choice). (4) Burkholderia (cepacia) + colistin: R (intrinsically resistant to colistin/polymyxins). (5) Klebsiella + ampicillin: R (intrinsic chromosomal penicillinase).
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI intrinsic resistance tables.

questions.question: Antiviral susceptibility testing.

parts.text: What is the main difference between phenotypic and genotypic testing?
What are 2 chronic viral infections that can only be done by genotype?
What are 2 chronic viral infections that can be tested genotypically and phenotypically?
Viral CPE detection. What are 3 methods to detect viral growth if there is no CPE pattern?

questions.model_answer:
a) Main difference: phenotypic testing measures actual viral replication/inhibition in the presence of drug (e.g., plaque reduction assay) and reflects true drug susceptibility but is slow and technically demanding; genotypic testing sequences resistance-associated genes and infers susceptibility from known mutations - faster and more widely available but requires a validated genotype-phenotype correlation database and may miss novel mutations.
b) 2 chronic viral infections tested only genotypically in routine practice: (1) HIV, (2) Hepatitis B virus.
c) 2 chronic viral infections that can be tested both genotypically and phenotypically: (1) HIV, (2) CMV (also HSV for antivirals).
d) 3 methods to detect viral growth without classic CPE: (1) hemadsorption assay, (2) shell vial culture with immunofluorescent staining for early antigen, (3) electron microscopy or molecular detection (PCR) of culture supernatant.
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard clinical virology methodology.

questions.question: You have been advised that the manufacturer of your blood culture bottles has had issues with "false-negatives" from lots of blood culture bottles between January – August of 2012.

parts.text: What are 5 things you need to do?

questions.model_answer: 5 required actions: (1) Notify laboratory director/medical microbiologist and infection control immediately; (2) Identify and quarantine/pull all affected lots from use; (3) Review and retrospectively identify all patients whose cultures used the affected lots during the exposure period; (4) Recommend repeat blood cultures for patients with negative results from affected lots who remain clinically concerning for bacteremia; (5) Report the issue to the manufacturer and relevant regulatory body (e.g., Health Canada/FDA MedWatch) and document via the lab's quality/incident management system.
questions.beyond_mandell: Laboratory quality management practice.

questions.question: You want to implement a 2nd blood culture incubator.

parts.text: List 2 issues with verifying the new instrument.

questions.model_answer: 2 verification issues: (1) Ensuring equivalent time-to-detection/sensitivity for organism recovery compared to the existing incubator (parallel testing with known positive controls and clinical isolates across organism types including fastidious organisms); (2) Confirming temperature, agitation, and CO2/atmospheric calibration meet manufacturer specifications and are validated before clinical use.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI verification/validation practice for new laboratory instruments.

questions.question: Chart about introducing a new antimicrobial susceptibility test. Given data from the gold standard and how the next test compares to the gold standard.

parts.text: Asked to calculate very major, major and minor errors. Also categorical agreement.
What are the accepted errors for introducing a new test (% of VME, ME)? What is the minimum % categorical agreement required of the new test?

questions.model_answer:
a) Very major error (VME) = false susceptible (test calls resistant isolate susceptible, using reference as truth); Major error (ME) = false resistant (test calls susceptible isolate resistant); Minor error = discrepancy involving intermediate category (either method calls intermediate when the other calls S or R). Categorical agreement (CA) = % of isolates for which the new test and reference method give the same category (S/I/R).
b) Accepted performance criteria: VME <1.5% (some criteria allow up to 3% with confidence interval upper bound <7.5%), ME <3%, and minimum categorical agreement generally required is ≥90%.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M52/FDA guidance for antimicrobial susceptibility test device evaluation.

parts.text: List 4 recommendations for analyzing and preparing antibiograms as per CLSI?

questions.model_answer: 4 CLSI recommendations for antibiograms: (1) Include only diagnostic (non-surveillance/duplicate) isolates, with only the first isolate per patient per analysis period; (2) Report cumulative data based on a minimum of 30 isolates per organism; (3) Analyze and update data at least annually; (4) Do not use antibiograms alone to guide empiric therapy for individual patients without correlating with local epidemiology/patient-specific factors, and separate data by specimen source/patient population where relevant (e.g., ICU vs. non-ICU).
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M39 guideline for antibiogram preparation.

parts.text: What are 4 antibiotics that are not recommended for routine testing in CSF as per CLSI?

questions.model_answer: 4 antibiotics not recommended for routine CSF susceptibility testing/reporting per CLSI: (1) oral cephalosporins, (2) tetracyclines, (3) macrolides (e.g., erythromycin, clindamycin), (4) first- and second-generation cephalosporins (e.g., cefazolin, cefuroxime) - these do not achieve adequate CSF penetration and should not guide meningitis therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100 footnotes on agents not appropriate for CNS infection reporting.

parts.text: What is a method described by CLSI to confirm a KPC? What is 1 example of a false positive using this test?

questions.model_answer: CLSI-described confirmatory method for KPC: the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM), sometimes paired with EDTA-CIM to distinguish KPC (serine carbapenemase) from metallo-beta-lactamases. A recognized false positive: organisms that are carbapenemase-negative but hyperproduce AmpC or ESBL combined with porin loss can give an indeterminate/false-positive inactivation result.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100 carbapenemase detection methods.

parts.text: 3 nucleic acid amplification methods besides PCR.

questions.model_answer: 3 nucleic acid amplification methods besides PCR: (1) Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), (2) Transcription-mediated amplification (TMA), (3) Nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (NASBA) (strand displacement amplification is also acceptable).
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard molecular diagnostics methodology.

questions.question: Your lab is using African green monkey cells for viral culture. There is a request for enterovirus culture. The sample inoculated with the patient's sample is already showing CPE after 1 day. On examination of other un-inoculated cells, there is already CPE. On EM, it looks like a herpesviridae.

parts.text: What virus is causing the CPE?
What are the implications for the patient sample inoculated in the contaminated bottle?

questions.model_answer:
a) The CPE seen in the uninoculated control cells (herpesviridae morphology on EM, rapid onset) indicates the African green monkey (Vero-type) cell line itself is contaminated with a latent/adventitious herpesvirus, classically simian cytomegalovirus (SV/simian herpesvirus, e.g., cercopithecine herpesvirus) - a well-recognized contaminant of primate cell lines, not the patient's virus.
b) Implications: the patient sample result is invalid/uninterpretable for enterovirus (cannot distinguish true enterovirus CPE from contaminant CPE); the specimen must be re-tested using fresh, verified/quality-controlled cell culture (or an alternative method such as enterovirus PCR), and the contaminated cell line lot must be discarded and the incident reported to quality/lab management.
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard virology cell-culture quality control principles.

questions.question: MALDI-TOF.

parts.text: 3 bacteria or bacterial groups that the MALDI has trouble identifying.
1 way in which these limitations can be improved.

cohort_answer.text: E coli + shigella sp; Strep pneumoniae + mitis group.

parts.text: 4 ways to differentiate Staphylococcus and Micrococcus in the lab.

questions.model_answer: Differentiate Staphylococcus from Micrococcus by: (1) Modified oxidase test - Micrococcus positive, Staphylococcus negative. (2) Bacitracin (0.04 U) susceptibility - Micrococcus susceptible, Staphylococcus resistant. (3) Furazolidone susceptibility - Staphylococcus susceptible, Micrococcus resistant. (4) Anaerobic acid production from glucose (OF/anaerobic tube) - Staphylococcus ferments glucose anaerobically, Micrococcus is oxidative only (no anaerobic growth/acid).
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard clinical microbiology bench methods (CLSI/ASM Manual of Clinical Microbiology), not covered in Mandell narrative text.

questions.question: Administrators tell you that you need to cut costs in the lab by $50,000. You review the urine culture bench in an attempt to streamline workup. The technologist asks how to work-up the following organisms further:

parts.text: GNB, ox negative, non-swarming, beta-hemolytic
GNB, ox negative, swarming, indole positive
GPC, cat negative, PYR positive

questions.model_answer:
a) GNB, oxidase negative, non-swarming, beta-hemolytic: consistent with E. coli (most common urinary pathogen) - report as presumptive E. coli from urine with typical colony morphology, proceed directly to AST without full biochemical ID to save cost.
b) GNB, oxidase negative, swarming, indole positive: swarming Proteus is either P. mirabilis (indole negative) or P. vulgaris (indole positive) - indole positive here identifies it as Proteus vulgaris (or related indole-positive Proteeae); report presumptive ID with AST.
c) GPC, catalase negative, PYR positive: presumptive Enterococcus species - report as "Enterococcus sp." without further speciation for routine urine isolates, proceed to AST (ampicillin/vancomycin panel).
questions.beyond_mandell: Cost-saving presumptive urine culture workup schemes are laboratory practice guidance (CLSI/ASM), not in Mandell.

parts.text: For Staphylococcus aureus, what are 2 different methods to test for beta-lactamase production?

questions.model_answer: Two methods to detect beta-lactamase production in S. aureus: (1) Nitrocefin (chromogenic cephalosporin) disk test - colour change from yellow to red/pink indicates hydrolysis. (2) Acidimetric/iodometric penicillin test (e.g., clover-leaf/zone-edge test) - bacteria grown near a penicillin disk show a fuzzy/hazy zone edge on prolonged incubation due to beta-lactamase induction.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI-recommended phenotypic beta-lactamase detection methods.

questions.question: A child was recently vaccinated for influenza (few days ago). He has been well but has had mild rhinorrhea. NPW positive for influenza A, influenza B and adenovirus. You review the controls and both negative controls were OK, and multiple other clinical samples on the run were negative.

parts.text: What is the most likely explanation?

questions.model_answer: Most likely explanation: the child recently received a live attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine (LAIV/FluMist), which contains attenuated influenza A and B strains; nasopharyngeal shedding of the vaccine strains is detected by PCR shortly after administration, producing true-positive influenza A and B results that reflect vaccine virus rather than wild-type infection. The concurrent adenovirus positivity likely represents a true co-infection causing the mild rhinorrhea. Assay controls being appropriate argues against a technical/contamination problem.

questions.question: Molecular station: Real time PCR to interpret (looked like the sample was negative, but the internal control for the sample had a weird curve and cycle time of 40).

parts.text: Describe.
What would you do to follow up?

questions.model_answer: Describe: the patient sample target is negative, but the internal (extraction/inhibition) control shows an abnormal amplification curve with a very late cycle threshold (Ct ~40, near the assay cutoff) - this indicates the internal control has failed or is borderline, raising concern for PCR inhibition or extraction failure rather than a confirmed true-negative result. Follow-up: repeat the extraction and PCR, and/or retest a dilution of the extract (e.g., 1:10) to dilute out potential inhibitors; if the internal control remains inadequate, report the result as invalid/indeterminate and request a repeat specimen rather than reporting a negative result.

parts.text: List 4 characteristics of this test.

questions.question: You are part of your hospital's antibiotic stewardship program and you want to publish a cumulative antibiogram.

parts.text: Name 4 principles to be respected in the development of cumulative antibiogram

questions.model_answer: Principles for developing a cumulative antibiogram: (1) Include only isolates tested for clinical/diagnostic purposes (exclude surveillance cultures). (2) Include only the first isolate per patient per analysis period, regardless of susceptibility profile (deduplication). (3) Include a species/organism only if a minimum of 30 isolates were tested during the period, to ensure statistical validity. (4) Compile and update the antibiogram at least annually, and report only routinely tested antimicrobial-organism combinations (using standard CLSI interpretive criteria).
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M39-A4 guideline for cumulative antimicrobial susceptibility testing data.

questions.question: Clsi ast for : amp, septra, fluoro (intestinal), 3+ ctx (extra intestinal)

parts.text: Clsi ast for : amp, septra, fluoro (intestinal), 3+ ctx (extra intestinal)

questions.model_answer: CLSI recommends routine susceptibility testing of Salmonella and Shigella be limited to ampicillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Septra), and a fluoroquinolone for isolates from intestinal (stool) sources. For extraintestinal isolates (e.g., blood, CSF), a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) should be added and reported, given the higher stakes of invasive infection.

parts.text: Spaulding classification. List the three and give an example for each.

questions.model_answer: Spaulding classification (device processing based on infection risk): (1) Critical items - contact sterile tissue or the vascular system; require sterilization (e.g., surgical instruments, implants). (2) Semi-critical items - contact mucous membranes or non-intact skin; require high-level disinfection (e.g., flexible endoscopes, laryngoscope blades). (3) Non-critical items - contact only intact skin; require low-level disinfection (e.g., blood pressure cuffs, stethoscopes).

questions.question: A child's stool culture grew an organism that was identified as Shigella flexneri by MALDI-TOF, which is what your lab uses for bacterial identification.

parts.text: Explain why this result may not be reliable?
Explain the concept of 'mass spectrum' and how it is used to identify bacteria.
Besides organism-related issues, name 3 general advantages and 3 general disadvantages for using MALDI-TOF in a microbiology lab. (Table format: Advantages 1/2/3, Disadvantages 1/2/3)

questions.model_answer:
a) The result may be unreliable because Shigella and Escherichia coli are genetically and proteomically nearly identical (Shigella is essentially a pathogenic clone/pathotype of E. coli); MALDI-TOF databases frequently cannot distinguish the two, risking misidentification of Shigella as E. coli (or vice versa). Confirmation with biochemical testing (e.g., non-motility, lysine decarboxylase negative) or molecular/serologic methods is recommended.
b) A mass spectrum is generated when a bacterial colony is ionized (matrix-assisted laser desorption) and the resulting charged protein fragments (mainly ribosomal proteins) are separated by time-of-flight based on their mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio; the resulting pattern of peaks is a species-characteristic "fingerprint" that is compared against a reference spectral database to generate an identification with a confidence score.
c) Advantages: (1) rapid turnaround (minutes per isolate vs hours to days for biochemical ID). (2) Low cost per test/reagent. (3) High throughput allowing many isolates to be processed simultaneously.
Disadvantages: (1) Cannot reliably differentiate very closely related species (e.g., Shigella/E. coli, Streptococcus mitis group/S. pneumoniae). (2) Requires an adequate pure culture/colony growth before testing (not usually direct from specimen). (3) Identification quality depends entirely on the comprehensiveness/currency of the reference database; novel or rare organisms may be misidentified or unidentified, and it does not provide susceptibility information.

parts.text: Name 4 advantages of new generation sequences over traditional sequencing

questions.model_answer: Advantages of next-generation sequencing (NGS) over traditional (Sanger) sequencing: (1) Much higher throughput - millions of sequences generated in parallel. (2) Lower cost per base sequenced. (3) Ability to sequence whole genomes/metagenomes without prior targeted amplification. (4) Ability to detect minor variants/mixed populations (quasispecies) within a sample, which Sanger sequencing cannot resolve.

parts.text: Give 4 uses of NGS for its use in ID and Public health

questions.model_answer: Uses of NGS in infectious diseases and public health: (1) Outbreak investigation and molecular epidemiology via whole-genome sequencing-based strain typing/phylogenetics. (2) Detection of antimicrobial resistance genes/mutations directly from isolates or specimens. (3) Metagenomic pathogen discovery/diagnosis of unexplained infections when standard testing is unrevealing. (4) Surveillance of viral evolution and variant tracking (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) to inform vaccine strain selection and public health response.

questions.question: 25. You are tasked with preparing a "cumulative antibiogram" for your hospital - what 4 features are essential for an antibiogram?

parts.text: What 4 features are essential for such an antibiogram?

cohort_answer.text: Analyze/report data annually; Only include species with ≥30 isolates; Include diagnostic, not surveillance, isolates; Only report results for drugs routinely tested; Only include the first isolate of the patient (regardless of body site); Calculate/report % susceptible (not % resistant). This is an annual summary of local susceptibility rates per CLSI Guidelines (2007)

questions.question: WGS.

parts.text: Name 4 advantages and disadvantages of new generation WGS
Name 4 applications of WGS in ID or Public Health

questions.model_answer: a) Advantages/disadvantages of WGS: Advantages: (1) Single-nucleotide resolution for outbreak/transmission tracing (2) Simultaneous detection of resistance genes, virulence factors, typing in one assay (3) Replaces multiple typing methods (MLST, PFGE, serotyping) (4) Growing database and decreasing cost. Disadvantages: (1) High capital/bioinformatics cost and need for trained personnel (2) Turnaround time still longer than phenotypic methods for acute management (3) Requires pure culture isolate (not usually direct from specimen) (4) Interpretation/standardization not yet harmonized across labs. b) Applications: (1) Outbreak investigation and transmission mapping (2) Antimicrobial resistance gene prediction (3) Public health surveillance of pathogen strains (e.g., TB, Salmonella) (4) Source attribution in foodborne outbreaks.

parts.text: A. Making an Antibiogram, name four requirements

cohort_answer.text: Precise method for measurement of resistance; Enough isolates; From clinically relevant sites; Access to many antibiotic testing; Representative data that is reviewed. Additional detail: analyze/present data annually; only include species if ≥30 isolates tested; diagnostic isolates only; results for routinely tested drugs only when finalized; first isolate per patient only; calculate percent susceptible (ignoring intermediate); S. pneumoniae use mening/non-mening breakpoints; Viridans list intermediate susceptibility to penicillin separately; S aureus calculate MRSA subset; use same MICs year to year

questions.question: explain MALDI TOF

parts.text: Shigella flexneri wit a clinical picture of dysentery - Why?
List 3 advantages and 3 disadvantages of this technology in a table format

questions.model_answer: MALDI-TOF: matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry - a bacterial colony is mixed with matrix, ionized by laser, and the resulting protein (mainly ribosomal) mass spectrum is compared to a reference database for species-level identification within minutes. Shigella flexneri with dysentery - why MALDI is problematic: Shigella spp. and E. coli are genomically/proteomically essentially the same species, so MALDI-TOF frequently misidentifies Shigella as E. coli and cannot reliably separate them; clinical/biochemical correlation (non-motile, lysine decarboxylase negative) is still needed. Advantages/disadvantages (table): Advantages - (1) rapid turnaround (minutes vs hours-days) (2) low reagent cost per test (3) high accuracy for most genus/species from pure culture. Disadvantages - (1) cannot reliably distinguish closely related species (e.g., Shigella/E. coli, S. pneumoniae/viridans strep) (2) does not provide antimicrobial susceptibility directly (3) requires isolated colony growth (culture-dependent) and high upfront instrument cost.

questions.question: Next generation sequencing (NGS) is a thing that you might have heard about (or not).

parts.text: What are four advantages over traditional sequencing?
What are four applications that have contributed to its adoption in public health and infectious diseases?

questions.model_answer: a) Advantages of NGS over traditional (Sanger) sequencing: (1) massively parallel/high throughput - whole genome in one run (2) lower cost per base (3) faster turnaround for whole-genome data (4) detects minor variant/mixed populations missed by Sanger. b) Applications driving adoption: (1) outbreak investigation and phylogenomic transmission tracing (2) antimicrobial resistance gene surveillance (3) novel pathogen discovery/metagenomics in culture-negative disease (4) vaccine and influenza strain surveillance.

questions.question: Explain MALDI-TOF.

parts.text: 4 key principles of MALDI-TOF and bacterial identification
List 3 advantages and disadvantages

cohort_answer.text: Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization-Time of Flight. Sample mixed with matrix on MALDI target, dried/crystallized; desorption/ionization with laser generates singly protonated ions; ions accelerated at fixed potential, separated by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z); charged analytes detected/measured using time of flight (TOF); characteristic spectrum (peptide mass fingerprint, PMF) generated. Advantages: Fast; Accurate; Less expensive than molecular/immunological methods; trained personnel not required. Disadvantages: High initial equipment cost; limited in identifying new strains (requires spectral database with matching PMFs); doesn't provide antibiotic susceptibility.

questions.question: List 2 disadvantages for the following testing regarding CMV:

parts.text: Culture
Serology IgM/IgG
PCR

questions.model_answer: a) Culture: (1) Slow turnaround (shell vial still takes 1-2 days, conventional culture longer). (2) Lower sensitivity than PCR, especially for blood/plasma viremia; does not reflect viral load well. b) Serology IgM/IgG: (1) Cannot distinguish reactivation/reinfection from primary infection reliably (IgM can persist or reappear). (2) Not useful in immunocompromised hosts who may fail to mount antibody response, and does not indicate active/ongoing replication. c) PCR: (1) Lack of standardization between labs/assays historically (different results across platforms, though improved with WHO international standard). (2) Detects DNA without necessarily indicating clinically significant disease (can be positive with low-level subclinical viremia), cost and access.

questions.question: Lyme disease modified double tier testing vs standard double tier testing

parts.text: Explain how MDTT is different from SDTT
Name 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages for MDTT

questions.model_answer:
a) SDTT (standard two-tier testing) uses a sensitive whole-cell (sonicate) EIA first, followed by IgM and IgG Western blot as the confirmatory second tier if the EIA is positive/equivocal. MDTT (modified two-tier testing) replaces the Western blot second tier with a second, different EIA (e.g., a VlsE C6-peptide EIA), so the result is two sequential EIAs rather than EIA-then-immunoblot.
b) Advantages: (1) more objective, standardized result (EIA is less subject to interobserver interpretation than Western blot) (2) faster turnaround and easier to automate. Disadvantages: (1) less long-standing clinical validation/experience than the traditional Western blot approach (2) still a two-step, two-test process so does not reduce testing cost or resolve poor sensitivity in early (localized) disease.

parts.text: Describe the components of C. diff testing
What is the limitation to NAAT testing clinically?

questions.model_answer: a) Components of C. diff testing (multi-step algorithm): (1) Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) EIA - sensitive screening test detecting the common antigen (present in toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains). (2) Toxin A/B EIA - specific for active toxin production, confirms clinically significant disease. (3) NAAT/PCR (e.g. for tcdB gene) used to arbitrate discrepant GDH+/toxin- results (three-step algorithm), or clinical correlation with symptoms. b) Limitation of NAAT testing: NAAT detects the toxin gene, not active toxin production, so it cannot distinguish true infection from asymptomatic colonization - leading to overdiagnosis/overtreatment if used as a standalone test in patients tested without clear clinical indication.

questions.question: C diff: multi test algorithm explain, limitations to NAAT only testing.

parts.text: C diff: multi test algorithm explain, limitations to NAAT only testing.

questions.model_answer: Multi-test algorithm: begin with GDH EIA (sensitive screen for common antigen present in both toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains); if positive, follow with toxin A/B EIA (specific for active toxin, confirms disease); if GDH and toxin EIA results are discrepant (GDH+/toxin-), arbitrate with NAAT (e.g. PCR for tcdB) - this three-step approach improves both sensitivity and specificity compared to any single test. Limitation of NAAT alone: detects the toxin gene (potential for toxin production) rather than active toxin, so cannot differentiate true infection from asymptomatic colonization, risking overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment when used as a standalone test.

questions.question: PM 7. Your organization uses MALDI-TOF for identification of bacteria. Girl presents with bloody diarrhea and reports Shigella flexneri

cohort_answer.text: Shigella too similar to E. coli (metabolically-challenged E. coli, same ribosomal proteins) - MALDI not reliable. Mass spec: colony placed on matrix, laser causes desorption/ionization of rRNA macroprotein; fragments ionized and accelerated in electromagnetic field, hit detector based on mass:charge ratio (bigger proteins = slower flight, time of flight TOF); spectra unique fingerprint compared to standardized database. Advantages: rapid identification, limited need for lab personnel, highly accurate, less subjective than biochemicals. Disadvantages: organism needs to be in database, does not give susceptibility patterns, expensive machine, unable to identify very closely related organisms (e.g. Strep mitis/oralis, E. coli/Shigella).

questions.question: C difficile

parts.text: Describe two tier testing and its rationale
Why may NAAT not be a great stand alone test?
List 3 intravenous antibiotics that can be dosed 3 times weekly with dialysis sessions

questions.model_answer: a) Two-tier testing: start with a sensitive screening test (GDH EIA, which detects the common antigen present in both toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains), followed by a specific confirmatory test (toxin A/B EIA) only if the screen is positive; rationale is that GDH alone is sensitive but not specific for toxigenic disease, while toxin EIA alone is specific but insensitive, so combining exploits the high negative predictive value of GDH with the specificity of toxin detection, improving overall accuracy and reducing overdiagnosis compared to NAAT alone. b) NAAT alone limitation: detects the toxin gene (tcdB), not active toxin expression, so cannot distinguish true CDI from asymptomatic carriage, leading to overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment. c) Three IV antibiotics dosed thrice weekly post-dialysis: (1) Vancomycin (renally adjusted, given post-HD). (2) Ceftazidime. (3) Daptomycin (also cefazolin acceptable) - all commonly dosed after each dialysis session (3x/week) due to dialyzability/renal clearance.

How to interpret test?

cohort_answer.text: Germ tube test. A rapid presumptive identification of C. albicans can be made by placing organism in serum and observing germ tube formation (small projections appearing within 90 min); used to differentiate C. albicans (and C. dubliniensis) from other Candida spp. Interpretation: sample placed in tube with sheep serum, incubated 2-4h, drop placed on slide with KOH prep - see filamentous outgrowth extending from yeast cells; positive germ tube test = C. albicans (or C. dubliniensis), based on non-constricted germ tube arising from yeast; false-negative and false-positive germ tube formations may occur; remainder of speciation relies on physiologic parameters rather than morphology.

questions.question: Immunocompromised patient with suspected invasive aspergillosis. You order a galactomannan assay

parts.text: What are 3 potential factors which could modify the result of the galactomannan assay, and how do they change sensitivity and specificity?
What two investigations would you now consider to confirm diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis?

cohort_answer.text: Decrease sensitivity: patient with CGD/Job syndrome; concomitant use of antimould agents; source of sample from serum. Decrease specificity: PipTazo and AmoxClav (historically, less of an issue now); other fungi (Penicillium, fusarium, histo); chemo (increases false positive due to gut translocation from mucositis); COPD (colonization with aspergillus); neonates (dietary intake or cross-reacting antigens with bacteria like Bifidobacterium); IVIG (1 study found false+ galactomannans post IVIG). Confirmatory investigations: CT chest +/- other imaging depending on symptoms; BAL specimens with tissue specimen for histopathology/cytology and fungal culture; galactomannan.

questions.question: Brucella plate manipulated on open bench.

parts.text: Name three high-risk activities in lab.
Name 3 aspects of management of high risk exposure

cohort_answer.text: High-risk exposure defined as: 1) direct personal exposure (sniffing cultures, direct skin contact, mouth pipetting, inoculation, spraying into eyes/nose/mouth); 2) working on open bench with open Brucella culture plate or close proximity (across open bench or within 5 feet); 3) presence during procedures that might aerosolize organisms (vortexing, catalase testing). Low-risk = present in lab during exposure but not meeting high-risk definition. Management: Step 0: risk assessment for all exposed workers; Step 1: offer PEP to all high-risk exposures (Doxycycline 100mg BID + rifampin 600mg daily x3 weeks, unless rifampin-resistant strain then add TMP-SMX DS BID to doxy; can give PEP to low-risk exposure if immunocompromised/pregnant, sometimes up to 6 months post-exposure); Step 2: surveillance for symptoms x6 months; Step 3: serologic follow-up (baseline, 6, 12, 18, 24 weeks post-exposure). (MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep. 2008;57(2):39)

questions.question: C difficile

parts.text: Describe two tier testing and its rationale
Why may NAAT not be a great stand alone test?

cohort_answer.text: Step 1 - testing for both glutamate dehydrogenase antigen (found on all C difficile isolates) and toxin A/B using enzyme linked immunoassay: GDH - high sensitivity, lower specificity; Toxins - high specificity, low sensitivity. Step 2 - NAAT testing to confirm presence of C diff toxin gene specific to toxigenic strains (highly sensitive so can rule out infection if negative but does not discriminate between toxin producing and non-toxin producing, colonizing C difficile). Want NAAT testing to follow up if discordant results between GDH and toxin antigens - more expensive but more specific for toxigenic strains, and sensitive
